title: Use Elimination Rules to Narrow a Decision
subtitle: Remove clearly unfit options before comparing what remains.
description: Define a few decision constraints, eliminate options that clearly fail them, then compare the smaller remaining set without pretending arbitrary thresholds are universal rules.

lifeOsSource.hack: When a decision has too many options, write the constraints that really matter, remove options that clearly violate them, and compare only what survives.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: List the viable options, write two to four constraints that are genuinely relevant to this decision, eliminate only options that clearly fail a constraint, inspect what remains for missing information and trade-offs, then choose the next reversible test or decision step.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which constraint removed an option, what uncertainty remains among the survivors, and what is the smallest next step that would improve the decision?

faq.question: Should every decision use numeric cutoffs?
faq.answer: No. Use a number only when the constraint is genuinely numerical, such as a hard budget or deadline. Do not invent precision merely to make the decision look objective.

faq.question: What if an eliminated option could still be valuable?
faq.answer: Check whether the constraint is truly mandatory. If it is, eliminate the option. If it is only a preference, keep the option and compare the trade-off instead of disguising a preference as a hard rule.

intro.html: Elimination is useful when a decision has accumulated too many plausible options. The aim is not to manufacture certainty. It is to remove choices that clearly cannot satisfy the constraints you already have, so attention can move to the smaller set that deserves real comparison.

sections.title: 1. Define the decision and the real constraints
sections.html: Write the decision in one sentence and list the constraints that would genuinely make an option unacceptable: a fixed budget, an immovable date, a required capability, a legal or safety boundary, or another condition you can defend. Keep preferences separate from hard constraints.

sections.title: 2. Eliminate only clear failures
sections.html: Review each option against the constraints. Remove it only when the failure is clear enough to explain in one sentence. If the evidence is missing, mark the uncertainty instead of treating an assumption as a failed test.

sections.title: 3. Compare the survivors
sections.html: Once the list is smaller, compare the remaining options on the trade-offs that matter. Ask what is still unknown, which difference could change the choice, and whether two options are effectively equivalent for the current purpose.

sections.title: 4. Choose a decision or an information-gaining step
sections.html: If one option now fits clearly better, choose it. If the remaining uncertainty could change the result, take the smallest reversible action that produces useful information: ask for a quote, run a small test, request a missing fact, or set a short decision checkpoint.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace fabricated decision-time and satisfaction statistics, invented first-party observations, arbitrary universal numeric thresholds, and pseudo-optimized probe rules with a bounded elimination workflow for low-stakes decisions.
